CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the Washington table and keep drafting text, including enforcement language, without new unilateral concessions or new retaliation. Treat additional U.S. purchases as a closing element of a package that also lifts or schedules down existing Section 301 tariffs—not as a standalone gift. Do not escalate on tariffs or the Huawei/Meng track while the List 3 hike remains suspended and both sides are reporting progress on text.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is still ~$250B of Chinese exports (Lists 1–3, List 3 at 10%), and U.S. goods imports from China have fallen about 26% in the lookback window (IMPCH latest $34.5B vs $46.3B), so the export channel is already being hit. Firm-level pressure is also live: Meng Wanzhou remains in the Canadian extradition process after the Jan 28 DOJ charges, and Huawei is a core industrial-policy asset. That maps below the +0.5 CHN anchor because FX and financial-stability stress are not showing: CNY strengthened to about 6.71 from ~6.92, reserves ticked up to ~$3.11T, industrial production is still expanding (latest 105.4), and March factory PMI rebounded after a winter contraction. The immediate tariff-hike clock has been stopped twice (G20 90-day pause; Trump’s Feb 24 delay), and the April 3 Washington round reports progress on text, including enforcement, with no deal signed. Action should therefore stay near zero. Escalating now would risk restoring the 25% List 3 hike that Washington has twice postponed. Unilateral purchase commitments or a partial rollback would be premature: U.S. officials still treat tariff removal as the main U.S. concession, Trump has signaled he may keep the 25% on the first $50B, and the Chamber publicly said China is unlikely to accept a snap-back enforcement device unless current tariffs come off. Negotiate the package; do not close it on U.S. terms alone.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports still under Section 301; List 3 remains at 10% after two delays of the 25% hike
April 3 Washington talks report progress on text/enforcement but no signed deal; remaining gaps are IP, industrial policy, and how enforcement/tariff lift are sequenced
Huawei/Meng extradition and the Kovrig/Spavor detentions sit alongside talks and keep tech-sovereignty risk elevated
Bilateral goods flow already compressed (US IMPCH down ~26%); China-wide exports only mildly weaker and CNY/reserves stable
U.S. offer is mainly tariff relief in exchange for structural change; conceding purchases now without a tariff path would give away leverage

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Intensive Washington talks; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
U.S. imports from China down ~25.6% in the window; latest $34.5B vs $46.3B in Nov 2018.
CNY strengthened to 6.7098 on 2019-04-03 from ~6.92 in early October; no FX-stress signal.
China reserves excluding gold ~$3.114T, slightly higher over the window.

April 2: Chamber says chances of a deal are rising but this week is critical on enforcement and a plan to lift U.S. tariffs; China unlikely to accept snap-back tariffs unless current tariffs are removed.
April 3: Liu He in Washington; outstanding issues include IP protection and an enforcement mechanism; Kudlow says good headway but no deal yet.
March 2019 factory PMI rebound after late-2018/early-2019 contraction; stimulus beginning to show, even as ~$250B of Chinese exports remain tariffed.
